Regression interpretation review

OLS

OLS: coefficients

  • The intercept is the expected value of the dependent variable when all predictors are 0

  • Coefficient values represent the effect of a one unit change in that variable on the predicted value of the dependent variable

    • In multiple regression, each coefficient represents the effect of a one unit change while holding constant for the other variables in the model

OLS: coefficients

  • When a state is 0% urban, we expect 33 motor vehicle fatalities per 100,000 population

  • As % urban goes up by one, we expect a -0.215 unit decrease in motor vehicle fatalities.

OLS: predictions

  • If a state is 50% urban, then the expected number of vehicle fatalities is: \(33.374 + -0.215 \times 50 = 22.624\)

OLS: p-values

  • The p-value tells us the probability of seeing a coefficient absolutely this large if the null hypothesis is true. Here, the null hypothesis is that the OLS coefficient is zero.

  • Remember that the p-value is a function of both the standard error and the effect size.

OLS: p-values

  • There’s a less than .001 chance of seeing an intercept value this large if the true intercept is 0 (not really useful information here!)

  • There’s a less than .001 chance of seeing a coefficient this large on urban if the actual coefficient is 0

OLS: r-squared

  • The R-squared statistic tells us how much of the variation in the dependent variable is explained by all of the independent variables.

  • Its a proportion, so it ranges from 0 to 1

OLS: r-squared

  • The R-squared statistic says that about 29% of the variation in motor vehicle fatalities is explained by variation in % urban.

  • The adjusted R-squared term just includes a small penalty for each predictor added to the model. The interpretation is otherwise the same.

OLS with categories

OLS with categories

  • When we have categorical predictors, we’ll include k-1 dummy variables (“k” = the number of categories)

  • The coefficients for the remaining categories should be interpreted as an effect relative to the excluded group.

  • The intercept term is still the expected value when ALL predictors = 0

OLS with categories: coefficients

  • Northeast is the excluded group here. So the intercept is the average of the DV for a state in the northeast when urban = 0.

  • The expected value of the DV for the midwest is 5.379 higher than the northeast

  • The expected value of the DV for the south is 8.715 higher than the northeast

  • The expected value of the DV for the west is 8.718 higher than the northeast

  • A one unit increase in % urban is associated with a -0.218 drop in the DV

OLS with categories: predictions

  • If a state is 50% urban and is in the midwest, the expected value of the DV is: \(27.217 + -0.218 \times 50 + 5.379 = 21.696\)

  • If a state is 50% urban and is in the south, the expected value of the DV is: \(27.217 + -0.218 \times 50 + 8.715 = 25.032\)

OLS with categories: predictions

  • The interpretation of P-values and R-squared values are unchanged

OLS with an interaction

OLS with an interaction: coefficients

  • We include an interaction term when we want to test whether the effect of a one unit increase in X depends on some other value.

  • This changes the interpretation of the coefficients!

OLS with an interaction: coefficients

  • The coefficient on urban is the effect of percent urban when South=0

  • The coefficient labeled southSouth is the difference between south/non-south when urban is 0

  • The coefficient labeled urban:southSouth is the difference between the slope when south = 0 compared to when south = 1.

OLS with an interaction: predictions

  • South/14% urban: \(27.877 + -0.158\times 14 + 12.678 + -0.127 \times 14 = 36.565\)

  • South/13% urban: \(27.877 + -0.158\times 13 + 12.678 + -0.127 \times 13 = 36.85\)

  • Non-south/14% urban: \(27.877 + -0.158\times 14 = 25.665\)

  • Non-south/13% urban: \(27.877 + -0.158\times 14 = 25.823\)

OLS with an interaction: effects

  • Effect of % urban for a non-south state = \(25.665 - 25.823 = -0.158\)

  • Effect of % urban for a southern state = \(36.565 - 36.85 = -0.285\)

  • The difference in effects for southern vs. non-southern states: \(-0.285 - -0.158 = -0.127\) (this matches the coefficient on the interaction term!)

OLS with an interaction: p-values etc.

  • P-values/R-squared have the same interpretations here.

  • Note that the p-value on urban:southSouth is not significant at the .05 level, but the p-value on urban and south are.

  • We can’t reject the null hypothesis that the interaction effect is 0.

Logistic regression

Logistic regression

  • We use logistic regression when the dependent variable is dichotomous.

  • The (un-transformed) coefficients represent the effect of a one-unit change in X on the logged-odds of Y=1

  • Odds ratio (bottom table) represent the effect of a one unit change on the odds ratio that Y=1. (remember that this is multiplicative, so 2 means “the odds double” and .5 means “the odds are halved”

Logistic regression: coefficients

  • A one unit change in literacy increases the logged odds of democracy by 0.031

  • This effect is statistically significant at the .05 level.

Logistic regression: predictions

  • We can convert this to a probability by getting the linear prediction and then using the inverse logit function.

  • At 25% literacy, the logged odds of democracy are \(-2.492 + 0.031 \times 25 = -1.717\)

  • \(\frac{e^{-1.717}}{1+e^{-1.717}} = 0.15\) or about 15%

Logistic regression: predictions

  • Remember that the effects on probability are non-linear. So a one unit change will have a different impact at a higher or lower level of the IVs.

Logistic regression: odds ratios

  • Odds ratios are another way to interpret logit effects. Remember that the odds of an event are equal to \(\frac{p}{(1-p)}\) Odds ratios are… the ratios between odds. So:

  • A value of 2 means: the odds are multiplying by 2.

  • A value of 1 means: the odds are multiplying by 1 (no change)

  • A value of .5 means: the odds are being halved.

Logistic regression: odds ratios

  • Each one-unit increase in literacy increases the odds of democracy by 1.031

  • This can also be interpreted as a 3% change in the odds of democracy

  • Remember that, for odds ratios, the null hypothesis is that the value = 1. So if the confidence interval does not contain 1, we can reject the null.

Logistic regression: pseudo-R2

  • Logistic regression models don’t have a real residual, but there are measures of model fit called pseudo-R squared that are meant to offer a rough analog to R-squared in a linear model.

  • The lower three figures here are variations on the pseudo R-squared value. They’re calculated in slightly different ways, but they’re all based on comparing the log likelihood of this model to a “null model” with no predictors.
